paras: The lynching of Thomas Reese was the killing of a Black man, also called Samuel Long, by a crowd at Moultrie, Colquitt County, Georgia, on September 4, 1888. Accused of assault and attempted poisoning, he was taken after a court ordered him committed, then mutilated, hanged and shot in daylight by unmasked men.

According to a Bainbridge dispatch, Reese had lived for two years with William Reagan of Miller County and was accused of having "outraged" Mrs. Reagan in December 1887 and trying to kill her with strychnine. He fled, but a neighbor of Reagan found him in Randolph County, Alabama, captured him at Eufaula, and brought him to the Moultrie jail on Monday night.

By Tuesday afternoon several hundred men had gathered in the village, and a committing court heard the case at four o'clock. When Reese was ordered committed, the crowd, "in broad daylight and without mask or disguise," took him to the edge of a nearby swamp. There the men performed "a very unusual and terrible surgical operation" as "a warning to others of his class and race," hanged him from a limb, and riddled the body with bullets. The body was later cut down and buried; the dispatch said a hundred or more men had a hand in it.
No report of an inquest or of arrests appears in the coverage, and no participant was named.

The Savannah Morning News ran the dispatch on September 6 under the headlines "Lynchers in a Frenzy" and "A Negro Mutililated, Hung to a Tree and Then Shot." It treated the accusation as fact, said Reese had "freely admitted his guilt," called him "the demon," and described "terrible and swift justice." It added that some of the most prominent citizens of Miller County took part and that, though opposed to mob law, they did not feel to blame. No other newspaper account appears in the coverage.
The dispatch also says the capture aroused "the citizens of Mitchell county," a third county name beside Miller and Colquitt.

accounts.label: Bainbridge dispatch
accounts.gist: Reese, said to have freely admitted his guilt, was ordered committed after a hearing, then taken by an unmasked crowd that mutilated, hanged and shot him; the dispatch says the participants were certain of his identity and crime and did not feel to blame.
